title: Defence Medical Services: lessons from Ukraine and preparing the nation
label: 27 October 2026 · Defence Medical Services one-off session
summary: Witnesses from King's College London and International SOS told the Defence Committee that battlefield medicine has changed: medical facilities are now at risk, evacuation is constrained, and many casualties require prolonged care close to where they were wounded. The UK lacks the capacity, pre-agreed commercial arrangements and whole-of-nation planning to cope at scale. The witnesses urged fast action—using the defence readiness Bill, pre-contracted transport and stockpiles, clearer regulation for wartime practice, investment in research (blood far forward, non-compressible haemorrhage, diagnostics), and a single lead to integrate defence, NHS, private and voluntary sectors.

glossary.definition: Defence Medical Services — the military organisation responsible for healthcare for UK armed forces.
A proposed law to give Government emergency powers and pre-arranged access to private resources in wartime.
Training and methods to treat traumatic battlefield injuries at the point of wounding to save lives.
NATO’s mutual defence clause: an attack on one is treated as an attack on all.
Giving blood products close to the battlefield to treat severe bleeding before evacuation.

chapters.title: How Ukraine has changed battlefield medicine
chapters.takeaway: Medical facilities and staff are now at greater risk, evacuation is harder, and many casualties need prolonged care near where they were wounded.

turns.speaker: Jesse Norman
turns.text: Ukraine shows a different pattern of injuries and a different battlefield. Has the DMS learned the clinical lessons?

turns.speaker: Dr Darren Mann
turns.text: Yes—Ukrainian clinicians have shared experience directly. The big change is that medical facilities and staff can no longer be assumed safe.

turns.speaker: Jesse Norman
turns.text: Does that mean more protection for near-front medical units?

turns.speaker: Dr Darren Mann
turns.text: It means changing how we deliver care: more treatment needs to happen far forward, evacuation times are longer, and rail/road rather than air transport is routine.

turns.speaker: Dr Katie Geary
turns.text: We used to rely on rapid casevac. In Ukraine that’s constrained: surgical and trauma care must be pushed forward and become more ‘industrial’ in scale.

turns.speaker: Dr Darren Mann
turns.text: Also ethically, measures once seen as temporary—like tourniquets—may need to be permanent because limb salvage becomes impossible in prolonged care settings.

chapters.title: Capacity, private sector and voluntary organisations
chapters.takeaway: The UK lacks surge capacity and joined-up planning; private and voluntary providers could help but need pre-arranged contracts and integration.

turns.speaker: Emma Lewell
turns.text: Who should coordinate national planning so military, NHS, private and voluntary sectors work together?

turns.speaker: Dr Darren Mann
turns.text: The Cabinet Office, via civil contingencies, should lead a whole-of-nation plan; many transport and logistics assets are outside government visibility now.

turns.speaker: Ed Button
turns.text: International SOS can coordinate care, provide hands-on treatment and train staff. Other NATO partners already integrate industry as true partners; the UK lags behind.

turns.speaker: Graeme Downie
turns.text: Can commercial and voluntary groups plug gaps at scale?

turns.speaker: Ed Button
turns.text: They can help, but their capacity isn’t infinite. The problem is converting capability awareness into pre-agreed contracts and funding—otherwise you’re at the back of the international queue.

turns.speaker: Dr Katie Geary
turns.text: Voluntary groups have a role, but they often lack clear link points into government planning. We must include them in exercises so we know what they can do.

turns.speaker: Michelle Scrogham
turns.text: Would mobilisation of reservists affect private providers’ workforce?

turns.speaker: Ed Button
turns.text: Not significantly for reputable providers; commercial organisations plan to maintain capacity. But staffing at national scale would require regulatory adjustments.

chapters.title: Transport, stockpiles and regulation
chapters.takeaway: We need pre-arranged access to trains, ships and aircraft, better stockpiles and flexible regulation for wartime practice—do it now, not after a crisis.

turns.speaker: Mike Martin
turns.text: Should the defence readiness Bill allow pre-arranged requisitioning of transport like trains and planes?

turns.speaker: Dr Darren Mann
turns.text: Yes—we should agree terms and service-level arrangements in peacetime rather than requisition at the last minute; requisition is legally strong but planning ahead gets better value.

turns.speaker: Ed Button
turns.text: Multimodal transport will be essential. The question is getting ahead of capacity and contracting now.

turns.speaker: Mike Martin
turns.text: What about stockpiles—how much should we hold?

turns.speaker: Dr Darren Mann
turns.text: Some sovereign stockpiling is needed—many critical items are manufactured overseas. A rule of thumb is around 120 days plus pre-agreed manufacturing and supply agreements.

turns.speaker: Derek Twigg
turns.text: Has pandemic experience made procurement and regulation simpler for emergencies?

turns.speaker: Dr Darren Mann
turns.text: Not enough. Derogations—temporary relaxation of regulations—helped in covid and are needed again. But they must be planned, so clinicians can act without breaching professional rules in crisis.

turns.speaker: Graeme Downie
turns.text: Can local charities be relied on?

turns.speaker: Ed Button
turns.text: They can help, but only if someone asks them and coordinates them ahead of time; otherwise their capacity is invisible until it’s needed.

chapters.title: Research, training and clinical priorities
chapters.takeaway: Immediate R&D and training should focus on prolonged far-forward care, TCCC training, blood forward, non-compressible haemorrhage and tackling antimicrobial resistance.

turns.speaker: Ian Roome
turns.text: Which research priorities would save the most lives quickly?

turns.speaker: Dr Darren Mann
turns.text: Work that accepts prolonged in-field care: what can be done far forward, what equipment to send to the casualty, and honest prioritisation when resources are scarce.

turns.speaker: Ed Button
turns.text: TCCC training is a high-impact, low-cost priority—training large numbers reduces deaths on the frontline, as other nations have shown.

turns.speaker: Dr Katie Geary
turns.text: Focus on survivability and return-to-function metrics, point-of-care diagnostics for resistant infections, blood far forward and reach-back telemedicine to support far-forward personnel.

turns.speaker: Ian Roome
turns.text: What stops research reaching the frontlines?

turns.speaker: Dr Katie Geary
turns.text: Fragmented accountability: procurement, NICE, royal colleges and regulators all matter. You need a sponsored pathway from research to adoption and planned derogations for wartime use.

turns.speaker: Ian Roome
turns.text: Is pay and retention a problem for military medics?

turns.speaker: Ed Button
turns.text: Pay is a risk for retention, but broader support—housing, veteran treatment and career pathways—matters too. Many stay for purpose rather than pay.

chapters.title: Ethics, prioritisation and the need for a national debate
chapters.takeaway: At scale, tough prioritisation choices are inevitable; government must lead an open discussion about wartime healthcare priorities and the moral choices involved.

turns.speaker: Derek Twigg
turns.text: If thousands are wounded, will the NHS prioritise service personnel over civilians?

turns.speaker: Dr Darren Mann
turns.text: We need an honest national debate. In an existential war the priority is to return service personnel to the fight; that likely means two channels of care and use of private sector beds for military patients.

turns.speaker: Dr Katie Geary
turns.text: That’s a major cultural and ethical shift. Ukraine shows we may need to accept different outcomes and to plan for palliative care on the battlefield for some injuries.

turns.speaker: Ed Button
turns.text: All of this only works if exercised now. Without pre-planning you’re knitting things together at the last minute and will lose out on scarce resources.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you could make the Government act, what would you ask and when?

turns.speaker: Dr Darren Mann
turns.text: Create a single organ with responsibility to integrate DMS, NHS, private and voluntary sectors and drive a national wartime medical plan—start now.

turns.speaker: Ed Button
turns.text: Provide fiscal support to DMS to enable pre-contracted private capacity and treat industry as a partner—not an enemy of public provision—immediately.

turns.speaker: Dr Katie Geary
turns.text: Commission an honest gap analysis against a Ukraine-type scenario, identify costs and partners, and don’t put the whole bill on DMS.
